results.summary: This Wokwi design builds a simple flip-flop from two cross-coupled NAND gates, with two switches as inputs and a light as output. The first switch acts as an enable, after which the second switch toggles the light on and off. It is intended as a first Wokwi project and a basic logic-gate exercise. The documentation is minimal and the external hardware list mentions a 7-segment display, which does not match the described light output.

This project is a Wokwi template intended to test a 7-segment display with switches. It exposes eight input pins and eight output pins, but the documentation consists only of the words "test" for both the description and the test procedure. External hardware listed is switches and a 7-segment display. There is not enough information to determine what logic, if any, the design implements.

This Wokwi design uses an 8-way DIP switch and combinational logic to display the letter L on a 7-segment display. Four specific switches feed an XOR gate and an AND gate, whose outputs are combined by a further AND gate to drive three segment outputs. The intended test is to toggle those four switches so that exactly one of the first pair and both of the second pair are active. It is a beginner logic-gate exercise, and the documentation is otherwise sparse.

This Wokwi design drives a 7-segment display from four switches, with the decimal point blinking at 1 Hz. The bottom four switches are used to turn on individual segments. It requires a 7-segment board and switches as external hardware. The documentation is very brief and the external hardware field still contains the template placeholder text.

This project is described as a test of a 7-segment display and switches, with six input pins and three output pins. Both the description of operation and the test instructions consist only of the word "test". External hardware listed is a 7-segment display and buttons. The documentation is too thin to determine what the design actually does.

This Wokwi design implements a simple multiplexer with two select lines and four data inputs, producing one output. The title calls it a 4:1 MUX while the description says 4:2, and the test table labels the pins inconsistently, so the exact configuration is ambiguous. No external hardware is required. The documentation is brief and partly contradictory.

This design contains a 3-bit linear-feedback shift register and a NAND gate, built for the Austrochip 2025 workshop. The NAND of inputs a and b appears on output 0, while the inverted LFSR state is presented on outputs 5 through 7. Switches for the inputs and LEDs for the outputs are the only external hardware needed. It is a small teaching design demonstrating basic sequential and combinational logic.

This project is labelled as a test project and provides four inputs a through d with their complements on four outputs. The description and test instructions repeat that it is a test project, and the test section states there are no IO pins despite the pin list. No external hardware is specified beyond the template placeholder. The documentation is essentially empty, so the design cannot be characterised beyond the inverter function implied by the pin names.

This project is described only as a test for submission, with two input pins and no output pins listed. The description and test instructions are one-line placeholders, and the external hardware field simply says "Test". There is no information about what the design does or how it should behave. The documentation is effectively absent.

This project is a template with four input pins and four output pins, described only as "created" and tested by giving inputs. No external hardware is required. The documentation gives no indication of the logic or function implemented. It appears to be an empty starting point rather than a complete design.
